[{:db/id 17592186124509 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d68af87f-be02-55a7-9b78-0da04db4e309"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d68af87f-be02-55a7-9b78-0da04db4e309" :question/id #uuid "d68af87f-be02-55a7-9b78-0da04db4e309" :question/math-academy-id "q-79345" :question/problem "Consider the matrices given below. Find $\text{dim(Null}(A))+\text{dim(Null}(B))+\text{dim(Null}(C)).$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "The dimension of the null space of a matrix is the number of non-pivot columns in the matrix. 

Also, all of the given matrices are in row echelon form.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- The matrix $A$ has $1$ pivot column and $2$ non-pivot columns (namely, the $2$nd and $3$rd columns). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=2.
$$

- The matrix $B$ has $3$ pivot columns and $1$ non-pivot column (namely, the $4$th column). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(B))=1.
$$

- The matrix $C$ has $3$ pivot columns and $1$ non-pivot column (namely, the $3$rd column). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(C))=1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))+\text{dim(Null}(B))+\text{dim(Null}(C))=2+1+1=4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f77f73c8-a6f1-5686-8eae-81626a3ac1d9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/eb/ebe962cc3394e0839d77fba922a5a7f56f31201f6926ef8b4236c1f82edd2e90.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$5,$ as shown above. What is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle?" :question/worked-solution "Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =10+l+\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $10,$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<10.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =100-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =100 \\ {l}^{2} & =50 \\ l & =5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=5\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,5\sqrt{2})$ | $5\sqrt{2}$ | $(5\sqrt{2},10)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $8$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So $l=5\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5\sqrt{2}) & =10+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{100-(5\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =10+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{100-50} \\  & =10+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{50} \\  & =10+5\sqrt{2}+5\sqrt{2} \\  & =10+10\sqrt{2} \\  & =10(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100029 :answer-field/correct "answer-dade38b2-d19e-5e1f-a69c-803c56722835" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bbdb68bd-b484-51c4-a434-8a6450e1553a" "answer-602e5323-47b5-567c-ad05-2e0f14c6bd42" "answer-dade38b2-d19e-5e1f-a69c-803c56722835" "answer-81a1d39e-ffa3-5851-9280-ef0749290fad" "answer-16d0883d-37ec-5524-9e37-0ebd4d8a596b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bbdb68bd-b484-51c4-a434-8a6450e1553a" :answer/id #uuid "bbdb68bd-b484-51c4-a434-8a6450e1553a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10(1+2\sqrt{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-602e5323-47b5-567c-ad05-2e0f14c6bd42" :answer/id #uuid "602e5323-47b5-567c-ad05-2e0f14c6bd42" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10(1+3\sqrt{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dade38b2-d19e-5e1f-a69c-803c56722835" :answer/id #uuid "dade38b2-d19e-5e1f-a69c-803c56722835" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10(1+\sqrt{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-81a1d39e-ffa3-5851-9280-ef0749290fad" :answer/id #uuid "81a1d39e-ffa3-5851-9280-ef0749290fad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10(1+\sqrt{3})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-16d0883d-37ec-5524-9e37-0ebd4d8a596b" :answer/id #uuid "16d0883d-37ec-5524-9e37-0ebd4d8a596b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5(1+4\sqrt{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e33bb576-2a78-5fb1-8965-49bc676e2392" :question/id #uuid "e33bb576-2a78-5fb1-8965-49bc676e2392" :question/math-academy-id "q-84644" :question/problem "![](images/64/643d8218715b65def0d9fd274c50b18c76cfbea35cd3dc70f3cdbb5c5b16b6f8.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$2,$ as shown above. What is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle?" :question/worked-solution "Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =4+l+\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $4,$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<4.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =16-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =16 \\ {l}^{2} & =8 \\ l & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=2\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,2\sqrt{2})$ | $2\sqrt{2}$ | $(2\sqrt{2},4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $3$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=2\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2\sqrt{2}) & =4+2\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{16-(2\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =4+2\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{16-8} \\  & =4+2\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{2} \\  & =4+4\sqrt{2} \\  & =4(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7d676937-e9eb-5b1f-9a5a-f6981fa3e2b6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7d676937-e9eb-5b1f-9a5a-f6981fa3e2b6" :answer-field/id #uuid "7d676937-e9eb-5b1f-9a5a-f6981fa3e2b6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-165e90cc-3b0d-5a02-a5a3-8e2d3d8588ed" :answer-field/choices ["answer-35dfa7d4-3b02-58c0-ad0c-6812b20c5dd1" "answer-165e90cc-3b0d-5a02-a5a3-8e2d3d8588ed" "answer-b08dd26b-63ed-5c34-a8e4-74444069711e" "answer-c1eabd82-920e-5aa0-b2c1-c63c5538278b" "answer-ef21318a-633e-5e82-8e9e-01f49a6a7ff5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-35dfa7d4-3b02-58c0-ad0c-6812b20c5dd1" :answer/id #uuid "35dfa7d4-3b02-58c0-ad0c-6812b20c5dd1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4(1+2\sqrt{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-165e90cc-3b0d-5a02-a5a3-8e2d3d8588ed" :answer/id #uuid "165e90cc-3b0d-5a02-a5a3-8e2d3d8588ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4(1+\sqrt{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b08dd26b-63ed-5c34-a8e4-74444069711e" :answer/id #uuid "b08dd26b-63ed-5c34-a8e4-74444069711e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4(2+\sqrt{3})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c1eabd82-920e-5aa0-b2c1-c63c5538278b" :answer/id #uuid "c1eabd82-920e-5aa0-b2c1-c63c5538278b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8(1+\sqrt{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ef21318a-633e-5e82-8e9e-01f49a6a7ff5" :answer/id #uuid "ef21318a-633e-5e82-8e9e-01f49a6a7ff5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8(1+\sqrt{3})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a9e9c021-fc29-5d89-a4ff-166a4f01dd84" :question/id #uuid "a9e9c021-fc29-5d89-a4ff-166a4f01dd84" :question/math-academy-id "q-84649" :question/problem "Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius

![](images/29/296e866a3104f0d2a7891726274578bcdffb84853ce896e8723e2b742d22ac27.png)

Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =10\sqrt{2}+l+\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $10\sqrt{2},$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<10\sqrt{2}.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =200-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =200 \\ {l}^{2} & =100 \\ l & =10\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=10$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,10)$ | $10$ | $(10,10\sqrt{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $11$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=10$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10) & =10\sqrt{2}+10+\sqrt{200-{10}^{2}} \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+10+\sqrt{200-100} \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+10+\sqrt{100} \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+10+10 \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+20 \\  & =10(2+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}

"63d7b221-5dbf-5fb1-b55e-24803c54cfbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-86380" :question/problem "Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius $10\sqrt{2}.$ If the hypotenuse of the triangle lies along the diameter of the semicircle, find the maximum possible area of the triangle." :question/worked-solution "We first draw a picture of the situation:

![](images/17/172826a7fa27ac8957f120e15622cf0c96b0e8df66e5f6fd3d7d99ab0b32c5f0.png)

Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $20\sqrt{2}$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<20\sqrt{2}.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 800-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ {l}^{2} & =\frac{800}{2} \\ {l}^{2} & =400 \\ l & =20\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=20$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,20)$ | $20$ | $(20,20\sqrt{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $25$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=20$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(20) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 20\cdot \sqrt{800-{(20)}^{2}} \\  & =10\cdot \sqrt{800-400} \\  & =10\cdot \sqrt{400} \\  & =10\cdot 20 \\  & =200.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-04564310-aef1-5572-80f0-0e88d49a5152"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-04564310-aef1-5572-80f0-0e88d49a5152" :answer-field/id #uuid "04564310-aef1-5572-80f0-0e88d49a5152" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-904dde19-8dc3-5432-80ad-2c1c137aafba" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5319f4ad-15cf-555e-aa17-f39d7212a5e8" "answer-e2149821-7718-5f16-85d2-5599e78ce659" "answer-904dde19-8dc3-5432-80ad-2c1c137aafba" "answer-d92ad90d-da23-5fff-85e4-1da26bf2a05e" "answer-50ba2075-ff36-56d5-92fd-c143a5d90b53"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5319f4ad-15cf-555e-aa17-f39d7212a5e8" :answer/id #uuid "5319f4ad-15cf-555e-aa17-f39d7212a5e8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "120\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e2149821-7718-5f16-85d2-5599e78ce659" :answer/id #uuid "e2149821-7718-5f16-85d2-5599e78ce659" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "160" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-904dde19-8dc3-5432-80ad-2c1c137aafba" :answer/id #uuid "904dde19-8dc3-5432-80ad-2c1c137aafba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "200" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d92ad90d-da23-5fff-85e4-1da26bf2a05e" :answer/id #uuid "d92ad90d-da23-5fff-85e4-1da26bf2a05e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "280" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-50ba2075-ff36-56d5-92fd-c143a5d90b53" :answer/id #uuid "50ba2075-ff36-56d5-92fd-c143a5d90b53" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "80\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7ba89d20-58fc-5947-9d86-d842de2f0086" :question/id #uuid "7ba89d20-58fc-5947-9d86-d842de2f0086" :question/math-academy-id "q-344587" :question/problem "![](images/f8/f88b6c506d909cce64eef23c71acaed15e382c55571f02048e0c9c616d75544e.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius $8,$ as shown above. Find the maximum possible area ${A}_{\text{max}}$  of the triangle. Do not round the answer.

${A}_{\text{max}}=$ 
 {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $16$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<16.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{A}^{′}(l)=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}}.
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 256-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{l}^{2} & =256 \\ {l}^{2} & =128 \\ l & =8\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=8\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,8\sqrt{2})$ | $8\sqrt{2}$ | $(8\sqrt{2},16)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $12$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=8\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area ${A}_{\text{max}}$  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{max}}=A(8\sqrt{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{256-(8\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{128} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 64\cdot 2 \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c876964c-ac3b-5bc2-8e7a-39e0baa2db2f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7ba89d20-58fc-5947-9d86-d842de2f0086" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134291 :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le z\le 2{x}^{2},\,0\le y\le 2xz\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133925 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-78d73ab6-dc58-5b09-8f0f-74be4ef20e0b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134127 :question/worked-solution "![](images/c1/c1853c772e219f53a0b394bd0b50beea6b33c451afc453983cdccb1df333c5ea.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 4-x-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/06/0620f8f25174cb71528049341669458c68a7ccfdd3ff76b5f62c878307080419.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 4-x-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}12xz\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-z}12xz\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-z}12xz\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{4-x-z}12xz\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}12xz[y]_{y=0}^{y=4-x-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}12xz(4-x-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(48xz-12{x}^{2}z-12x{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(48xz-12{x}^{2}z-12x{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}(48xz-12{x}^{2}z-12x{z}^{2})\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[24x{z}^{2}-6{x}^{2}{z}^{2}-4x{z}^{3}]_{z=0}^{z=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(64x-24{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(64x-24{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[32{x}^{2}-8{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(32-8)-0 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281291 :question/problem "Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}6y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281319 :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

and $D$ is a finite region in $xz$-plane enclosed between the $x$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the curve $z+{x}^{2}=1$ in the first quadrant." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-78d73ab6-dc58-5b09-8f0f-74be4ef20e0b" :question/id #uuid "78d73ab6-dc58-5b09-8f0f-74be4ef20e0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-164349" :question/problem "![](images/78/78c5b7d059cac1d2ad94edf93a3d9317a62e5c1d1c88a4be29c49bbe9dac5f39.png)

Given that $R$ is the type III region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}V=$" :question/worked-solution "For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=2$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=6.$

![](images/a0/a03d6986874a543bc21d274433b5268444f2487aea198834d379f004a7d85e79.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,2\le y\le 6\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-x.
$$

![](images/06/06e8986d493efbe696751db410f84490ba634c9f68feaa03aa0bf9d71593feb3.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-x\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{2}^{6}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}[{\int }_{2}^{6}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}{x}^{2}[y]_{y=2}^{y=6}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b4d91747-a788-57b5-b27b-550a878336f2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "7b9e6797-8ad6-50af-aa3b-75e9f9aa6e0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-96689" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 11 & -1 \\ 2 & 8 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above. Which of the following is a basis of the eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =7.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 11 & -1 \\ 2 & 8 & 5\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -1 \\ 2 & 8 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0=0 \\ {x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 8 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-4{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the required basis is

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.

For example, consider the function shown in the graph below. 

![](images/19/197834de138cb2e05a3af391bbeec1279ad8bfddfb277b881e5e3eeb49bcb73a.png)

The graph has a peak at the point $A$ where $x=0.$ We say that the function has a **local maximum** when $x=0.$ We also say that the point $A$ is a **local maximum point** of the function. 

This means that we can take an open interval of $x$-values around $x=0$ such that $A$ will be the highest point on the graph in this interval. 

![](images/d5/d522b4b0a59ff328399493bc12a770af2d99a1587b2826accb9835d7463ef9ba.png)

Similarly, the graph has a valley at the point $B$ where $x=2.$ We say that the function has a **local minimum** when $x=2.$ We can also say that the point $B$ is a **local minimum point** of the function.

This means that we can take an open interval of $x$-values around $x=2$ such that $B$ will be the lowest point on the graph in this interval. 

![](images/e2/e2a92d4217e1eebcc724e48cca273d2e707731ded914207e59fff149b46b4dcc.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153407 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to looking at the function $y=f(x)$ that we saw earlier.

![](images/19/197834de138cb2e05a3af391bbeec1279ad8bfddfb277b881e5e3eeb49bcb73a.png)

The point $A$ where $x=0$ is a local maximum of $f(x)$ because we can draw an open interval around $x=0$ such that the point $A$ is the highest point on the graph. One such interval is $x\in (-0.5,0.5),$ shown below:

![](images/d5/d522b4b0a59ff328399493bc12a770af2d99a1587b2826accb9835d7463ef9ba.png)

Everywhere in this interval, the value of the function is *less than or equal to* $f(0),$ the largest value of the function in this interval. We can write this mathematically as

$\qquad$ $f(x) \leq f(0)$ for all $x\in(-0.5, 0.5).$

Similarly, the point $B$ where $x=2$ is a local minimum of $f(x)$ because we can draw an open interval around $x=2$ such that the point $B$ is the lowest point on the graph. One such interval is $x\in (1.5,2.5),$ shown below:

![](images/e2/e2a92d4217e1eebcc724e48cca273d2e707731ded914207e59fff149b46b4dcc.png)

Everywhere in this interval, the value of the function is *greater than or equal to* $f(2),$ the smallest value of the function in this interval. We can write this mathematically as

$\qquad$ $f(x) \geq f(2)$ for all $x\in(1.5, 2.5).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153406 :tutorial/content "Can a point on a graph be both a local minimum *and* a local maximum?

To answer this question, let's consider the function $f(x)$ given by the graph below. 

![](images/0c/0cec91d9ec8e108ee4836e816aae63722fc4c09d997790eaf283cd3e2a9c4bc6.png)

Now consider the point where $x=2.$ Our goal is to determine which type of extremum it is. To do this, we consider the values of $f(x)$ in the open interval $(1.5, 2.5),$ shown below.

![](images/c6/c6cf1a6237c50d5c2b651937ca46b9ae52a08dafb831d76b27ddb068d37dd501.png)

Now, notice the following:

- The point where $x=2$ is a local maximum because $f(x) \le f(2) \:$ for all $\: x \in (1.5,2.5)\quad {\color{\green}\checkmark}$

- The point where $x=2$ is a local minimum because $f(x) \ge f(2) \:$ for all $\: x \in (1.5,2.5)\quad {\color{\green}\checkmark}$

Therefore, $x=2$ is both a local maximum *and* a local minimum of $f(x)!$ 

This might seem strange. But, notice that $x=2$ lies within an interval where the function is constant. This is a special case where a particular point is both a local minimum and a local maximum." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152350 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186326906 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/264cb888010525848f647669653d34383535dd32e6ac264927105540c3b85f9f.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=-(x-y).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):\pi \le x\le 2\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying the Green's Theorem we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xdx-(x-y)dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}^{0}dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186326911 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/73/73bf9b973e50c540a873f4f1a44d936474e4c49d7041a330902508a840645009.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({x}^{3}+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}+2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):y\le x\le 2-y,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{3}+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-y}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}-4xy]}_{y}^{2-y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(2-y)^{2}-4(2-y)y-{y}^{2}+4{y}^{2}]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8{y}^{2}-12y+4)\,dy \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2}-3y+1)\,dy \\  & =4{[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}+y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4[\frac{2}{3}-\frac{3}{2}+1] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134074 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/7c/7ca4b6fe3a5a16c4004c75b0e4524cc3b42550cb2413d5b8e1c21a1d53cee902.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3})dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{8{y}^{3}}{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{16}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{[{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot {2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186244257 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

In the quadrilateral $ABCD$ above, determine the measure of $∠C.$" :question/worked-solution "A quadrilateral has $n=4$ sides. Therefore, the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral  must be 

$$
\begin{aligned}{180}^{∘}\cdot (n-2) & ={180}^{∘}\cdot (4-2) \\  & ={180}^{∘}\cdot 2 \\  & ={360}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding up the internal angles and solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C+m∠D & ={360}^{∘} \\ x+{90}^{∘}+3x+6x & ={360}^{∘} \\ 10x+{90}^{∘} & ={360}^{∘} \\ 10x & ={270}^{∘} \\ x & ={27}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠C & =3x \\  & =3({27}^{∘}) \\  & ={81}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186104050 :answer-field/correct "answer-55f686c3-4dc7-5ee6-94df-392ace9f44b3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b20abdd4-a291-58d8-b13c-b588f3c268d0" "answer-a4ab1399-f698-5779-856e-01b204aa3767" "answer-b25b8a4a-c870-5c94-9647-8973446f4945" "answer-0dc54541-63d3-5382-8d61-ad8fb7a2df0c" "answer-55f686c3-4dc7-5ee6-94df-392ace9f44b3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b20abdd4-a291-58d8-b13c-b588f3c268d0" :answer/id #uuid "b20abdd4-a291-58d8-b13c-b588f3c268d0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{34}^{∘}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a4ab1399-f698-5779-856e-01b204aa3767" :answer/id #uuid "a4ab1399-f698-5779-856e-01b204aa3767" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{63}^{∘}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b25b8a4a-c870-5c94-9647-8973446f4945" :answer/id #uuid "b25b8a4a-c870-5c94-9647-8973446f4945" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{68}^{∘}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0dc54541-63d3-5382-8d61-ad8fb7a2df0c" :answer/id #uuid "0dc54541-63d3-5382-8d61-ad8fb7a2df0c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{75}^{∘}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55f686c3-4dc7-5ee6-94df-392ace9f44b3" :answer/id #uuid "55f686c3-4dc7-5ee6-94df-392ace9f44b3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{81}^{∘}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8d216a5f-ca4b-530d-81c3-76f09a214af9" :question/id #uuid "8d216a5f-ca4b-530d-81c3-76f09a214af9" :question/math-academy-id "q-4316" :question/problem "![](images/fa/fa797de4c7edfb4e4c4bc4eab40e8443f832c0407f08fd9d9ae28730c468a71e.png)

:question/worked-solution "Remember that the sum of the interior angles of a polygon with $n$ sides is ${180}^{∘}\cdot (n-2).$

To find the number of sides in our polygon, we start by setting up the following equation:

$$
{180}^{∘}\cdot (n-2)=3\,{960}^{∘}
$$

Now, we solve for $n,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{180}^{∘}\cdot (n-2) & =3\,{960}^{∘} \\ n-2 & =\frac{3\,{960}^{∘}}{{180}^{∘}} \\ n-2 & =22 \\ n & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polygon has $n=24$ sides." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d8f0acf3-60c9-5fe9-a760-cefa37eb9b66"] :db/ensure "The graph of $y=7f(2x-2)+5,$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by applying **some** of the following transformations:

- $(\text{T}1)$ - Translate up by $5$ units

- $(\text{T}2)$ - Stretch by a scale factor of $7$ parallel to the $y$-axis

- $(\text{T}3)$ - Translate right by $1$ unit

- $(\text{T}4)$ - Stretch by a scale factor of $0.5$ parallel to the $x$-axis

- $(\text{T}5)$ - Translate right by $2$ units

Which of the following could be a possible ordering of the appropriate transformations?" :question/worked-solution "To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the function:

$$
y=7f(2x-2)+5=7f(2(x-1))+5
$$

To get $y=7f(2(x-1))+5,$ we could apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}4).$ Stretch $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}=0.5$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(2x).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}3).$ Translate $y=f(2x)$ right by $1$ unit to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(2(x-1)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}2).$ Stretch $y=f(2(x-1))$ by a scale factor of $7$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=7f(2(x-1)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}1).$ Translate $y=7f(2(x-1))$ up by $5$ units to get the graph of 

$$
y=7f(2(x-1))+5.
$$

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

$\,$ $(\text{T}4)\to (\text{T}3)\to (\text{T}2)\to (\text{T}1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-014d1aa7-6876-598e-b36b-73f23d2e7df3"] "![](images/9f/9f8a8203c3684107378ff709e3c2675a767cbbfe03fc93b3665abcaa7ac13054.png)

Compute the value of $\theta \in [0,\pi]$ for which the polar curve $r=e^{-\theta}$ (shown above) has a horizontal tangent, given that

$$
x'(\theta)=-e^{-\theta}(\cos\theta+\sin\theta), \qquad
y'(\theta)=e^{-\theta}(-\sin\theta+\cos\theta).
$$" :question/worked-solution "We have a horizontal tangent when

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)} = 0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
y'(\theta) = 0 \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad x'(\theta) \neq 0.
$$

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives $y'(\theta)$ and $x'(\theta).$ 

We're given that

$$
x'(\theta)=-e^{-\theta}(\cos\theta+\sin\theta), \qquad
y'(\theta)=e^{-\theta}(-\sin\theta+\cos\theta).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta$ where $y'(\theta)=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-\theta }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \theta  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only one belongs to the required domain, namely

$$
\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether any candidates have $x'(\theta) = 0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solutions into $x'(\theta)$ and check that $x'(\theta) \neq 0.$ If $x'(\theta) = 0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-{e}^{-\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =-{e}^{-\pi /4}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi /4} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, our curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

y'(\theta) = \cos(2\theta)+\sin(2\theta).
$$" :question/worked-solution "We have a vertical tangent when

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
x'(\theta) = 0 \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad y'(\theta) \neq 0.
$$

To find the vertical tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives $y'(\theta)$ and $x'(\theta).$ 

We're given that

$$
x'(\theta) = \cos(2\theta)-\sin(2\theta), \qquad
y'(\theta) = \cos(2\theta)+\sin(2\theta).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta$ where $x'(\theta)=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ) & =1 \\ 2\theta  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi  \\ \theta  & =\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{n\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only two belong to the required domain, namely

$$
\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{8},\qquad \theta_2 = \dfrac{5\pi}{8} .
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether any candidates have $y'(\theta) = 0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solutions into $y'(\theta)$ and check that $y'(\theta) \neq 0.$ If $y'(\theta) = 0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting $\theta_1 =\dfrac{\pi}{8},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 =\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ is a valid solution.

- Substituting $\theta_2 =\dfrac{5\pi}{8},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{5\pi }{8}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore, $\theta_2 = \dfrac{5\pi}{8}$ is also a valid solution.

Therefore, our curve has vertical tangents at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{8}, \dfrac{5\pi}{8}.$

$$

$$

 
So, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, our curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$

$$

$$

Now, recall that the slope of the tangent line to a polar curve is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}.

Therefore, at the points $A$ and $B,$ we must have

$$
\dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)} = 0.
$$

For this equation to be satisfied for some value of $\theta,$ we require that the *numerator* is zero while the *denominator* is nonzero. Therefore, we must find the points where

$$
y'(\theta) = 0\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad x'(\theta) \neq 0.
$$

which is undefined. Points where $y'(\theta)$ and $x'(\theta)$ are both zero require further investigation.

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives $y'(\theta)$ and $x'(\theta).$ 

Doing this using the usual methods, we get

$$
x'(\theta)=-\sin\theta(2\cos\theta+1), \qquad 
y'(\theta)=2\cos^2\theta +\cos\theta - 1.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta$ where $y'(\theta)=0.$

Writing down the equation $y'(\theta) = 0$ and factoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1 & =0 \\ (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations: 

$$
2\cos\theta-1 = 0, \qquad \cos\theta + 1= 0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve the equation

$$
2\cos\theta-1 = 0,  \qquad 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.
$$

The solutions to this equation are 

$$
\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3}.
$$

- Then, we solve the equation

$$
\cos\theta + 1=0, \qquad 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.
$$

The solution to this equation is 

$$
\theta = \pi.
$$

Therefore, we have three candidate solutions:

$$
\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \qquad \theta_2 = \pi, \qquad \theta_3 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether any candidates have $x'(\theta) = 0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solutions into the expression for $x'(\theta).$ If $x'(\theta) = 0,$ further investigation is necessary.  

- Substituting $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+1) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+1) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(1+1) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =-\sqrt{3} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ is a valid solution.

- Substituting $\theta_2 = \pi,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+1) \\  & =-0\cdot (-1) \\  & =0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we draw *no conclusion* regarding $\theta_2 = \pi.$

- Substituting $\theta_1 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})+1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\sqrt{3} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is a valid solution.

We now make the following conclusions: 

- We have horizontal tangents where $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}.$ These correspond to the points $A$ and $B,$ respectively.

- This analysis gave no conclusion regarding the point where $\theta = \pi.$ We'll learn to deal with points like this in future lessons.

:question/id #uuid "8ba3cd0d-7f42-50d0-93f6-108a716173e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-84826" :question/problem "Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(-3,-2)$ and which passes through the point $(2,3)?$" :question/worked-solution "The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-3,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x+3=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(2,3),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=3$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5=2pt \\ 5=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =2pt \\ t & =\frac{5}{2p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =p{(\frac{5}{2p})}^{2} \\ 5 & =p\cdot \frac{25}{4{p}^{2}} \\ 5 & =\frac{25}{4p} \\ p & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+3=2(\frac{5}{4})t,\,y+2=(\frac{5}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+3=\frac{5}{2}t,\,y+2=\frac{5}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-46647a5c-2b95-53fe-940a-e6b35e9ddd8e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(3,-2),$ and passes through the point $(7,-6).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(3,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-3=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(7,-6),$ we can substitute $x=7$ and $y=-6$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ -4=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -4 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -4 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=2(-1)t,\,y+2=(-1){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-2t,\,y+2=-{t}^{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-829f2828-1700-5400-9439-0d028651d780"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "13a87bfd-ec89-5321-9298-2cba42bc0bbc" :question/math-academy-id "q-106506" :question/problem "Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x+1=2{t}^{2},\,y+3=4t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{x+1}{2},\,t=\frac{y+3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{y+3}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{x+1}{2}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{16} & =\frac{x+1}{2} \\ (y+3)^{2} & =16\cdot (\frac{x+1}{2}) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =8(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-314ab3a0-11b2-5836-a9a6-779f4e2cfc86"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-314ab3a0-11b2-5836-a9a6-779f4e2cfc86" :answer-field/id #uuid "314ab3a0-11b2-5836-a9a6-779f4e2cfc86" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6e7f9396-d71d-5308-95cc-a34867a20ca6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7c5d3114-e499-590c-baf7-861605384f54" "answer-2e072a8a-4c4e-573b-8869-941c8567a11b" "answer-7a134ec0-3a05-56eb-ad2c-0e83ebd565ee" "answer-dc78eb36-9d33-50e7-9b6c-c918281f4ed5" "answer-6e7f9396-d71d-5308-95cc-a34867a20ca6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7c5d3114-e499-590c-baf7-861605384f54" :answer/id #uuid "7c5d3114-e499-590c-baf7-861605384f54" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(x+1)^{2}=4(y+3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2e072a8a-4c4e-573b-8869-941c8567a11b" :answer/id #uuid "2e072a8a-4c4e-573b-8869-941c8567a11b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(x+1)^{2}=8(y+3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7a134ec0-3a05-56eb-ad2c-0e83ebd565ee" :answer/id #uuid "7a134ec0-3a05-56eb-ad2c-0e83ebd565ee" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(y+3)^{2}=-8(x+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dc78eb36-9d33-50e7-9b6c-c918281f4ed5" :answer/id #uuid "dc78eb36-9d33-50e7-9b6c-c918281f4ed5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(y+3)^{2}=4(x+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6e7f9396-d71d-5308-95cc-a34867a20ca6" :answer/id #uuid "6e7f9396-d71d-5308-95cc-a34867a20ca6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(y+3)^{2}=8(x+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-727c8803-de94-5b7f-a91c-cc70ef9900c0" :question/id #uuid "727c8803-de94-5b7f-a91c-cc70ef9900c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-84849" :question/problem "Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

"e38cbfdc-40f4-5e23-81ff-d9532344f653" :question/math-academy-id "q-118856" :question/problem "Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}$ and the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u=-{x}^{4}$,  then $\text{d}u=-4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{4}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-{x}^{4}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{-{a}^{4}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ae057d8d-edb0-54d6-852b-f3d8185d31f2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/f7/f78efc78b9f7cded50b29ba63855d81ff4e9ee8b7d12aa9673fac1cb7644e50a.png)

Find the total area $A$ of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=5{e}^{-|x|+1}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}5{e}^{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}5{e}^{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{x+1}{|}_{a}^{0}\,) \\  & =5{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0+1}-{e}^{a+1}) \\  & =5(e-0) \\  & =5e.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $5{e}^{-|x|+1}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x=5e.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }5{e}^{-|x|+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5e+5e \\  & =10e.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ba5aae1a-3e45-5846-af9a-9b9e31b42dfe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ba5aae1a-3e45-5846-af9a-9b9e31b42dfe" :answer-field/id #uuid "ba5aae1a-3e45-5846-af9a-9b9e31b42dfe" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d04d6f59-7d03-5768-bf23-8c1a24199af9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d04d6f59-7d03-5768-bf23-8c1a24199af9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d04d6f59-7d03-5768-bf23-8c1a24199af9" :answer/id #uuid "d04d6f59-7d03-5768-bf23-8c1a24199af9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186320878 :question/worked-solution "We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2}){|}_{a}^{0}\,) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}+\frac{3\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186320362 :answer-field/correct "answer-d16a7ece-3c28-5cdc-b1c9-a82826a0c636" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d16a7ece-3c28-5cdc-b1c9-a82826a0c636"] {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,5),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,5), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-5,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our cases, for $x\in (-5,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-(-x){e}^{3(-x-1)} \\  & =x{e}^{3(-x-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =(-1){e}^{3(-(-1)-1)}=-{e}^{3(0)}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-175c2fdb-c390-5385-bb9c-f23c3bd1dd27"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-175c2fdb-c390-5385-bb9c-f23c3bd1dd27" :answer-field/id #uuid "175c2fdb-c390-5385-bb9c-f23c3bd1dd27" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-19797644-81c9-5edc-8c9f-6d1f16ca9e89" :answer-field/choices ["answer-19797644-81c9-5edc-8c9f-6d1f16ca9e89"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-19797644-81c9-5edc-8c9f-6d1f16ca9e89" :answer/id #uuid "19797644-81c9-5edc-8c9f-6d1f16ca9e89" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186315064 :question/worked-solution "If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,8),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

- The function $f(x)$ is also continuous at $x=2.$ The graph can be drawn in the neighborhood of $x=2$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

To illustrate, let's consider the function $y=x^2$ whose graph is shown below. 

![](images/67/67ffd0b78845693b522100f4f0ba460cae6fedd796964b24708e320eab04ce29.png)

 

We can draw as much of the function $y=x^2$ as we want without taking our pencil off of the paper. Therefore, we say that $y=x^2$ is **continuous** at every point in its domain.

Let's compare this to the function $y=g(x)$ below:

![](images/a0/a07ccd15d14fa3eeb00a9c4ab07674c1c169e2a0d0a3e9fcb64798e9929e2ff9.png)

 

Notice that this function has a jump in its value at $x=0.$

It is *impossible* to draw $y=g(x)$ without taking the pencil off the paper to fill in the jump at $x=0.$ Therefore, we say that $y=g(x)$ has a **discontinuity** at $x=0.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069961 :tutorial/content "Now consider the function $y=h(x)$ below. This function has a discontinuity at $x=0,$ so it is not continuous over its entire domain.

![](images/4e/4e41ca41e4befba33c62da68666a8c4a2e2c7a19c79331360ae4bf124edafd50.png)

 

However, the function $h(x)$ may be continuous at other points, such as $x=1.$ 

To determine whether $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=1,$ we have to consider points in the **neighborhood** of $x=1.$ Roughly speaking, the *neighborhood of $x=1$* means the points on the curve that have an $x$-coordinate that's close to $1.$

Indeed, in the *neighborhood* of $x=1,$ we can draw the function $h(x)$ without taking the pencil off the paper. So, $h(x)$ is indeed continuous at $x=1.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068989 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162045 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-84533a55-9193-5a76-a277-23539897c843"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-84533a55-9193-5a76-a277-23539897c843" :question/id #uuid "84533a55-9193-5a76-a277-23539897c843" :question/math-academy-id "q-363663" :question/problem "$$

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{(-4)}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3} & 0 & \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f3a85cef-fa7c-5a3f-95d7-68572b164e28" "answer-field-6a1c4465-2c9b-5772-9efc-361ca67d4ae5" I. The discriminant of the equation is a perfect square.

II. The equation has only rational solutions.

III. The equation has only irrational solutions." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have $a=1,$ $b=2,$ and $c=-15.$ So, we calculate the discriminant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(2)^{2}-4(1)(-15) \\  & =4+60 \\  & =64\end{aligned}
$$

And $64={8}^{2}$ is a perfect square.

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. 

First, notice that our quadratic equation has rational coefficients. And, since the discriminant is a nonzero perfect square, the equation must have two rational solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065847 :answer-field/correct 17592186065849 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-8988f053-e75a-5c75-a866-50d1b2af5964" :question/id #uuid "8988f053-e75a-5c75-a866-50d1b2af5964" :question/math-academy-id "q-218746" :question/problem "The equation $2{x}^{2}+5x-9=0$ has{{field-1}}

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={5}^{2}-4(2)(-9) \\  & =25+72 \\  & =97\end{aligned}

First, we calculate the discriminant. We have $a=k,$ $b=4,$ and $c=2,$ so the discriminant is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(4)^{2}-4(k)(2) \\  & =16-8k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the values of $k$ such that the discriminant is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =0 \\ 16-8k & =0 \\ 8k & =16 \\ k & =\frac{16}{8} \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

[:db/retract 17592186220936 :answer-field/choices 17592186220940] [:db/retract 17592186220936 :answer-field/choices 17592186220941] {:db/id 17592186222042 :question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =L\{5t\}+L\{3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}=\frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186220936 :answer-field/correct "answer-9fb78983-301f-5651-9fb7-1ab6e18840f8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-83c7c20a-5a9a-5e9c-92d4-1db64ddad7aa" "answer-5c5f41d3-f5c2-5c17-99da-23a331941594" "answer-9a625c27-70a6-5cf6-bcf3-a7be0cbcc47f" "answer-9fb78983-301f-5651-9fb7-1ab6e18840f8" "answer-50798ffc-3732-5591-ba0b-04ece45c7da1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-83c7c20a-5a9a-5e9c-92d4-1db64ddad7aa" :answer/id #uuid "83c7c20a-5a9a-5e9c-92d4-1db64ddad7aa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5c5f41d3-f5c2-5c17-99da-23a331941594" :answer/id #uuid "5c5f41d3-f5c2-5c17-99da-23a331941594" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{4}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a625c27-70a6-5cf6-bcf3-a7be0cbcc47f" :answer/id #uuid "9a625c27-70a6-5cf6-bcf3-a7be0cbcc47f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{3}{(s-3)^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9fb78983-301f-5651-9fb7-1ab6e18840f8" :answer/id #uuid "9fb78983-301f-5651-9fb7-1ab6e18840f8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-50798ffc-3732-5591-ba0b-04ece45c7da1" :answer/id #uuid "50798ffc-3732-5591-ba0b-04ece45c7da1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{3}{(s-3)^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186390920 :question/problem "Consider a function $y(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{y(t)\}=Y(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{4t}y(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{4t}y(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$

$$

Now, recall that $Y(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$

$$

Find $BM$ given that the area of $△ACB$ is $49\,{cm}^{2},$ $AM=5\,cm,$ and $MC=9\,cm.$

(Figure not drawn to scale)" :question/worked-solution "The area of the triangle is defined as 

$$
A=\frac{b\cdot h}{2},
$$

 where $b$ is the base and $h$ is the corresponding height.

From the diagram, we see that the height is $h=BM,$ and the corresponding base is 

$$
b=AM+MC=14\,cm.
$$

Therefore, using the formula for the area, we can solve for the height as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 49 & =\frac{14\cdot h}{2} \\ 98 & =14\cdot h \\ h & =\frac{98}{14} \\ h & =7\,cm\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $BM=7\,\text{cm}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8da7771e-63f1-5e10-be3c-1af25ccedf2e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{coth}⁡x(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x+\operatorname{csch}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{coth}⁡x\cdot 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x+\operatorname{coth}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csch}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x+\operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{csch}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2\operatorname{cosh}⁡x+\operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{csch}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{csch}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x-\operatorname{csch}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d537a454-077e-5bec-8d5e-c804712b982d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Evaluate ${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "$$

First, recall the following identity:

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{csch}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡9$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{csch}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡9}{csch}^{2}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡9}{csch}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{coth}⁡u){|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡9} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡9)+\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡9}+1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡9}-1}+\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{9}^{2}+1}{{9}^{2}-1}+\frac{{4}^{2}+1}{{4}^{2}-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{41}{40}+\frac{17}{15}) \\  & =\frac{13}{240}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fca0c653-f489-5a0b-b300-4fbf7f846779"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fca0c653-f489-5a0b-b300-4fbf7f846779" :answer-field/id #uuid "fca0c653-f489-5a0b-b300-4fbf7f846779" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3d5ae3f1-9426-5b71-9c8a-39ff341b203d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-efbf3afe-ee5e-5490-a69f-dee8cd1d6186" "answer-3d5ae3f1-9426-5b71-9c8a-39ff341b203d" "answer-adaf5e80-f765-530e-bb4c-2a9cb2a2639f" "answer-f4838b2c-2ff8-52d4-bfdd-390ae6cc1518" "answer-e3b3d1f0-bf8f-570f-a904-dec2d7f66618"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-efbf3afe-ee5e-5490-a69f-dee8cd1d6186" :answer/id #uuid "efbf3afe-ee5e-5490-a69f-dee8cd1d6186" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{11}{120}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3d5ae3f1-9426-5b71-9c8a-39ff341b203d" :answer/id #uuid "3d5ae3f1-9426-5b71-9c8a-39ff341b203d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{13}{240}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-adaf5e80-f765-530e-bb4c-2a9cb2a2639f" :answer/id #uuid "adaf5e80-f765-530e-bb4c-2a9cb2a2639f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{13}{75}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f4838b2c-2ff8-52d4-bfdd-390ae6cc1518" :answer/id #uuid "f4838b2c-2ff8-52d4-bfdd-390ae6cc1518" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{23}{110}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e3b3d1f0-bf8f-570f-a904-dec2d7f66618" :answer/id #uuid "e3b3d1f0-bf8f-570f-a904-dec2d7f66618" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{45}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167138 :question/problem "$\int \operatorname{sech}⁡x(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x-2\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "$$

$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{coth}^{2}⁡x}{2{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "$$

$$

First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{coth}^{2}⁡x}{2{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {coth}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now we need to find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Then, we use the above identity to write the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {coth}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{csch}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{coth}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡(1)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡2 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{e}^{2}+1}{{e}^{2}-1}-\frac{{e}^{4}+1}{{e}^{4}-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{({e}^{2}+1)^{2}-({e}^{4}+1)}{({e}^{4}-1)}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{e}^{4}-1}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-40c090a2-44ae-5ef6-9984-cc694c4d8efa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-40c090a2-44ae-5ef6-9984-cc694c4d8efa" :answer-field/id #uuid "40c090a2-44ae-5ef6-9984-cc694c4d8efa" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-3a0d7365-f518-5311-a5f3-c5f826b81b2c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3a0d7365-f518-5311-a5f3-c5f826b81b2c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3a0d7365-f518-5311-a5f3-c5f826b81b2c" :answer/id #uuid "3a0d7365-f518-5311-a5f3-c5f826b81b2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2}}{{e}^{4}-1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ba7d332a-6786-594a-94f9-7b21daa8d15e" :question/id #uuid "ba7d332a-6786-594a-94f9-7b21daa8d15e" :question/math-academy-id "q-352941" :question/problem "$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}3\operatorname{sech}⁡(3x)\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities:

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{tanh}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x},\,\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}3\operatorname{sech}⁡(3x)\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{sech}⁡(3x)\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=3x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=3x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡8$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{sech}⁡(3x)\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}\operatorname{sech}⁡(u)\operatorname{tanh}⁡(u)\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡(u){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡8} \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡8)+\operatorname{sech}⁡(0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡8)}+1 \\  & =-\frac{1}{(\frac{8+{8}^{-1}}{2})}+1 \\  & =-\frac{1}{(\frac{65}{16})}+1 \\  & =\frac{49}{65}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-25b5f170-7d01-575f-9c9a-1bf9fe7b0568"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+1)$, find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{ln}⁡u,\,u=3x+1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{1}{3x+1}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{3}{3x+1}.\end{aligned}

$$
f=\operatorname{ln}⁡u,\,u=4-2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{4-2x}\cdot (-2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{4-2x} \\  & =-\frac{\cancel{2}}{\cancel{2}\cdot (2-x)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={-\frac{1}{2-x}|}_{x=1}=-\frac{1}{2-1}=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is $m=-1.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-499c195b-8d64-5d7d-9d3e-bb9baebdfb2e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-499c195b-8d64-5d7d-9d3e-bb9baebdfb2e" :answer-field/id #uuid
