$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the second of these integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u=1+{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }({-\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}|}_{0}^{a}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}+\frac{1}{(1+0)^{2}}) \\  & =-0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6cb888af-c468-5ec7-990d-1e6270a76de3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536007}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19e74ed4-4bf4-58a5-82f1-bb5ffa3a7eee" :answer/type {:db/id $$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{3}$,  then $\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{({e}^{{x}^{3}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{{a}^{3}}) \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

In our case, for $x\in(-6,0),$ we get

$$

**odd** $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

![](images/e2/e25e66141569f5324759eb15a1dcf8b143f5018cf35e957f7a212ba3b45b3556.svg)" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=4x$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
b_n = \dfrac{8}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{8}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{8\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have

$$
b_n = -\dfrac{8(-1)^n}{n}=\dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n} \cdot \sin(nx).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050730} {:db/id 17592186050929} {:db/id 17592186167283 :question/id #uuid "37a89f3d-e2cd-5d21-bb53-6d99da952356" :question/math-academy-id "q-340629"} {:db/id 17592186167284 :question/id #uuid "7a38bbe2-8cc7-5da0-8136-af259e1c0160" :question/math-academy-id "q-340708" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166956 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1a85c9c4-8563-55e0-9d4f-7d61d3be6243" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Sine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0288041e-13a5-5541-bbd8-c13988faf24e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/id 17592186427748} {:answer/id #uuid "319ba16a-7d74-5bcd-99b2-bc9850751276" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{(1-(-1)^{n})}{4\pi n}" :db/id 17592186427749} {:answer/id #uuid "7a9fb755-7be5-5ae8-be1c-cea88ce12977" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2(1+(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/id 17592186427750} {:answer/id #uuid "82973565-ede8-565e-a9ef-215aaa0446b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4(1+(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/id 17592186427751} {:answer/id #uuid "d703d305-1fef-58e0-ac9f-aedced6da080" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/id 17592186427752}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "d703d305-1fef-58e0-ac9f-aedced6da080" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/id 17592186427752} :answer-field/id #uuid "32a95669-d006-58f5-a342-6964952c273c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494 :db/ident :answer-field.type/select} :db/id 17592186164929}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186315034 :question/id #uuid "a94eebf7-ea68-5ac3-9351-043b927df6ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-340926"} {:db/id 17592186315083 :question/id #uuid $$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-3x+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-3x+2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[(-3x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)(-1)^{n}-2)=\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2).
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).

automatically.
In particular, if a $2\pi$-periodic function is *odd*, then its Fourier series has *sine terms only*.

A **Fourier sine series** uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval, say, $[0,\pi),$ but we want a full Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ (and then a $2\pi$-periodic extension to all real $x$).

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,12),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,12), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-12,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-12,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}-6(-x)) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =-(-4)^{2}-6(-4)=8.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0e3afe28-7b8e-5c73-9d90-38ba90dbb6e5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186540166}} {:db/id 17592186540129 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167270 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03bfdb40-b020-5871-af7f-669ab81b634f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{x}^{2}-2x" :db/id 17592186539484} {:answer/id #uuid "0d477725-039a-569b-974c-cc8168427bd5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{x}^{2}+2x" :db/id 17592186539506} {:answer/id #uuid "133cc9fe-58b4-5563-9de2-f20044a1ad82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}-2x" :db/id 17592186539516} {:answer/id #uuid "8d7a4ec2-f370-5681-81e3-c63a1d8a2f8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "|x{|}^{2}+2|x|" :db/id 17592186539719} {:answer/id #uuid "a721105a-d718-5aac-86a9-455b5f022623" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "|-{x}^{2}+2x|" :db/id 17592186539760}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539484} :answer-field/id #uuid "163adf1f-a5ba-53ac-95f1-d113394667f0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186164819}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "487df78e-b6e4-5124-9586-cb2ed967b312" :question/math-academy-id "q-338784" :question/problem "Let $F(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$" :question/worked-solution "If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7f36f74d-9ded-58b3-8942-de350905b5b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-340922" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=-3x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "745e2678-3dfd-5d17-a3ad-6185ef0d904f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186540119}} {:db/id 17592186540166 :step/content {:db/id 17592186315083 :question/answer-fields "![](images/18/1867a80955ae4b456cbcb011eefed96431f2b12926994942613eb947e55e38c6.png)

 

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$

- $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \, 2}f(x)$ exists

- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$" :question/worked-solution "By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $f(2)=2.$

- Statement II is false. From the graph, we can see that the left and right-sided limits are different:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x) & =2, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \, 2}f(x)$ does not exist.

- Statement III is false.  The graph of the function breaks at $x=2.$ It's impossible to draw the graph of $f(x)$ without taking our pencil off of the paper. Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous at $x=2.$

In conclusion, only statement I is true."} {:db/id 17592186048943} {:db/id 17592186051049} {:db/id 17592186514550} {:db/id 17592186069366 :question/id #uuid "544abde9-c223-5348-b980-33df85581d2d" :topic/math-academy-id 462} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069958 :tutorial/content "A function $f(x)$ is **continuous** over its entire domain if the graph of $y=f(x)$ can be drawn using a pencil and a piece of paper without taking the pencil off of the paper.

To illustrate, let's consider the function $y=x^2$ whose graph is shown below. 

![](images/67/67ffd0b78845693b522100f4f0ba460cae6fedd796964b24708e320eab04ce29.png)

We can draw as much of the function $y=x^2$ as we want without taking our pencil off of the paper. Therefore, we say that $y=x^2$ is **continuous** at every point in its domain.

Let's compare this to the function $y=g(x)$ below:

![](images/a0/a07ccd15d14fa3eeb00a9c4ab07674c1c169e2a0d0a3e9fcb64798e9929e2ff9.png)

Notice that this function has a jump in its value at $x=0.$

It is *impossible* to draw $y=g(x)$ without taking the pencil off the paper to fill in the jump at $x=0.$ Therefore, we say that $y=g(x)$ has a **discontinuity** at $x=0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Now consider the function $y=h(x)$ below. This function has a discontinuity at $x=0,$ so it is not continuous over its entire domain.

![](images/4e/4e41ca41e4befba33c62da68666a8c4a2e2c7a19c79331360ae4bf124edafd50.png)

However, the function $h(x)$ may be continuous at other points, such as $x=1.$ 

To determine whether $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=1,$ we have to consider points in the **neighborhood** of $x=1.$ Roughly speaking, the *neighborhood of $x=1$* means the points on the curve that have an $x$-coordinate that's close to $1.$

Indeed, in the *neighborhood* of $x=1,$ we can draw the function $h(x)$ without taking the pencil off the paper. {:db/id 17592186069961 :tutorial/content "Now consider the function $y=h(x)$ below. This function has a discontinuity at $x=0,$ so it is not continuous over its entire domain.

![](images/4e/4e41ca41e4befba33c62da68666a8c4a2e2c7a19c79331360ae4bf124edafd50.png)

However, the function $h(x)$ may be continuous at other points, such as $x=1.$ 

To determine whether $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=1,$ we have to consider points in the **neighborhood** of $x=1.$ Roughly speaking, the *neighborhood of $x=1$* means the points on the curve that have an $x$-coordinate that's close to $1.$

Indeed, in the *neighborhood* of $x=1,$ we can draw the function $h(x)$ without taking the pencil off the paper. So, $h(x)$ is indeed continuous at $x=1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "54ca4bef-1b8e-5315-85d4-0667910b332c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2640 :tutorial/title "Continuity at a Point"} {:db/id 17592186048143 {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$

$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$  select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$

Now, we compute the $1$st column of $U.$ It is given by:

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal.

Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to 

$$
{{field-3}}.
$$

Choosing ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by:

|  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | {{field-5}} |  |  |

that we can rewrite as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the two linearly independent solutions are already mutually orthogonal, we only need to normalize them. Hence, we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{10} \\ 2\sqrt{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186370697 :question/id #uuid "f5a19d61-895b-51bb-abe5-e33bbbd340f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-363836"} {:db/id 17592186381942 :question/id #uuid - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{10}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186381985 :question/id #uuid "8d1f0a35-56cb-5370-99fa-b599f7ccb0a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-363840"} {:db/id 17592186408019 :question/id #uuid - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423863 :question/id #uuid "bd607d3f-88f1-5057-a261-73a39b9023d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-363834"} {:db/id 17592186430360 :question/id #uuid </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443407 :question/id #uuid "c1d729e8-d1cb-584b-b25e-2da8d463c255" :question/math-academy-id "q-363831" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443408 :question/id #uuid "dd93c01d-3a4b-5e26-802f-bf34131bc696" :question/math-academy-id "q-363664" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{2}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186545815 :question/id #uuid "47b88835-9941-5b00-8cef-a75a2de591b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-363832"} {:db/id 17592186162043 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id Now, we compute the $1$st column of $U.$ It is given by:

Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

{{field-3}}.

that we can rewrite as:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}}.
$$

Next, we orthogonalize ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process to get the corresponding orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 0 & \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423861 :question/id #uuid "9d7c03f5-6a85-5299-a2e8-604190d0a4f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-363852"} {:db/id 17592186430359 :question/id #uuid - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{3}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186525985 :question/id #uuid "03ae1482-39ea-5fad-a59a-df13068a2393" :question/math-academy-id "q-363219" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$  select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$

Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
{{field-3}}.

Choosing ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by:

|  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}}.
$$

Next, we orthogonalize ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process to get the corresponding orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Let ${c}_{1}={b}_{1},$ then:

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{(-1)}{5}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186545827 :question/id #uuid "6ad1efca-7cc0-5d3a-adf8-070336e066c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-363849"} {:db/id 17592186048654} {:db/id 17592186049503} {:answer-field/choices 17592186162858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163233 :tutorial/content "We can compute a singular value decomposition (SVD) of any matrix! The algorithm for computing an SVD of a rectangular $m\times n$ matrix $(m\neq n)$ is similar to the algorithm for square matrices.

As an example, let's consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/f6/f65e0eee905da85ce0be4bbf39546c2b31c2bac082ff00a6a1d54fd5b89a4a4e.svg)

Notice that $A$ is a ${\color{blue}{3}}\times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix. So, to compute the SVD of $A,$ we must write

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T,
$$

where

- $\Sigma$ is a ${\color{blue}{3}}\times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal ${\color{blue}{3}} \times {\color{blue}{3}}$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix.

We proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.**  Find the singular values of $A.$ Computing the eigenvalues of $A^TA,$ we get

$$
\lambda_1 = 4, \qquad \lambda_2 = 2.
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are 

$$
\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1} =  2,  \qquad \sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2} =  \sqrt{2}.
$$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$). Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T \! A - \lambda_1 I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ and $(A^T \! A - \lambda_2 I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvectors 
![](images/07/07085f021218ff17060b3c1a9099e1cabad24b3d12269f97f1fe50d49b970f6b.svg)

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A.$ Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the first two columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $U$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix. However, we do not have the third singular value, so we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 
![](images/71/71f89dbcee33bce284b3085b872fdb9da2cc41166fe8a0bd26ef0bb5fe6876aa.svg) 
such that 
![](images/9e/9edc744372650e86c27f31ef15ac575cc8203803bdc5fe5730390727fd37146a.svg)
Solving this system, we get the following nonzero normalized solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

{:db/id 17592186385970}} {:db/id 17592186162948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163258 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find an SVD for the $2\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/32/325fa7080fdd5f7fc5723a2304aac049a938dfd1b490f09a7a2ceabb0b934db8.svg)

Directly applying the standard approach to $A$ could be problematic because it requires finding the eigenvalues of the $4\times 4$ matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

In such cases, it's usually more convenient to find an SVD of the transposed matrix $A^T$ and then take the transpose of the resulting SVD. In this case, we would only have to find the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

For example, if

$$
A^T = U \Sigma V^T
$$

is an SVD for $A^T,$ then

$$
A= \left(A^T\right)^T= \left(U \Sigma V^T\right)^T=V\Sigma^T U^T
$$

is an SVD for $A.$  

Going through our usual process, we find that an SVD for $A^T$ is

![](images/78/7802bcf50374a71efc4c0a7754c5628e88e7f1dfac345bc9e590cfcebd89d8d1.svg)

Taking the transpose of the above equation. we find that an SVD for $A$ is

![](images/77/77f464a1ce372dcd4e9aecb99b23342dee26fd5cf3f701ffa2fc858ebb4865b5.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "71ba93f6-01a1-54c4-bda4-b51b9b8dad77" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5110 :tutorial/title "The Singular Value Decomposition of a Transposed Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "e87c19a4-7e24-5962-880c-39d60fa71758" :step/math-academy-id 648304} {:db/id 17592186162951 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162045 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161839 :question/id #uuid "1b9d8b05-cdb6-555b-b68c-b46000bb6650" :question/math-academy-id "e-8798"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "566bda0f-f62d-581d-936d-baa8ae474e50" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050578}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162726} {:db/id 17592186162727} {:db/id 17592186370740} {:db/id 17592186370793} {:db/id 17592186423858} {:db/id 17592186423861} {:db/id 17592186430359} {:db/id 17592186525985} {:db/id 17592186545827}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Cases Requiring Orthogonalization"} :step/id #uuid "7cf890cb-057f-5300-9a99-426e3fb959db" :step/math-academy-id 648301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162948}} {:db/id 17592186385970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186385971 :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.

This happens, for example, when:

- an eigenvalue is repeated, or

- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.

In these cases, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  

For example, we solve an equation of the form

$$
(A^T A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0},
$$

or, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0, \qquad \mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0.
$$

- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  

This shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like

$$
\mathbf{v} = x\,\mathbf{b}_1 + y\,\mathbf{b}_2,
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are free variables.

- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  

We usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.

- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  

If the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.

- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  

After that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.

These unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$

**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:

- belong to the correct solution space,

- are mutually orthogonal, and

- have norm $1.$

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} :step/id #uuid "7dc02cbe-4a5d-5f2d-8ad3-baa5e8278916" :step/math-academy-id 648305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162946}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162227} {:db/id 17592186162858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163233 :tutorial/content "We can compute a singular value decomposition (SVD) of any matrix! "7cf890cb-057f-5300-9a99-426e3fb959db" :step/math-academy-id 648301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162948}} {:db/id 17592186385970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186385971 :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.

This happens, for example, when:

- an eigenvalue is repeated, or

- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.

In these cases, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  

For example, we solve an equation of the form

$$
(A^T A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0},
$$

or, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0, \qquad \mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0.
$$

- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  

This shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like

$$
\mathbf{v} = x\,\mathbf{b}_1 + y\,\mathbf{b}_2,
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are free variables.

- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  

We usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.

- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  

If the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.

- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  

After that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.

These unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$

**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:

- belong to the correct solution space,

- are mutually orthogonal, and

- have norm $1.$

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} :step/id #uuid "7dc02cbe-4a5d-5f2d-8ad3-baa5e8278916" :step/math-academy-id 648305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162946}} {:db/id 17592186162948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163258 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find an SVD for the $2\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by

In such cases, it's usually more convenient to find an SVD of the transposed matrix $A^T$ and then take the transpose of the resulting SVD. In this case, we would only have to find the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

For example, if

$$

$$
A= \left(A^T\right)^T= \left(U \Sigma V^T\right)^T=V\Sigma^T U^T
$$

is an SVD for $A.$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e2882521-8d21-5a7b-8813-60683b9344e3"} {:db/id 17592186408023 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408020 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a847e10-ad2a-5e19-bffe-4f473d1f4614" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407950} {:answer/id #uuid "53b3d1ac-5ba6-5b42-802f-34c001d2a3eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407952} {:answer/id #uuid "7ba9bbe0-a4bd-5d08-aca1-3c1661cf6c5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407966} {:answer/id #uuid "e36cd36f-f51a-505a-8f73-b691e55977cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407993} {:answer/id #uuid "e71af25d-d057-558a-8db8-29ad46847b17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407996}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407996} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e3568eb-62d3-583e-93bd-bbecf0a0149d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186408002}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "256724b0-7532-517f-89d9-acc3daa6cf56" :question/math-academy-id "q-98766" :question/problem "$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e4884cf0-a1fa-595d-912e-314992ac2509" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408024}} {:db/id 17592186408024 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408021 :question/answer-fields - $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e4884cf0-a1fa-595d-912e-314992ac2509" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408024}} {:db/id 17592186408022 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408019 :question/answer-fields - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}

A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ec7950f-72d8-5bef-a77f-3f5e2a3e06a0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186430364}} {:db/id 17592186430362 :step/content {:db/id 17592186430360 :question/answer-fields {{field-3}}.

|  |  | $2{x}_{3}$ |  |  |

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ac4c51ea-2c80-5f4f-b061-1215e274de99" :step/next {:db/id 17592186430363}} {:db/id 17592186430363 :step/content {:db/id 17592186430359 :question/answer-fields
