So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "15c5dca7-7c90-57e5-be91-60bf5e44e76b" :step/math-academy-id 657076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167786}} {:db/id 17592186167786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "4b9873f3-a548-5ea9-a86b-7682d0efa06b" :step/math-academy-id 657077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167782}} {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} {:db/id 17592186167788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166882 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166487 :question/id #uuid "35c3c9ba-60b0-5bcf-8e9c-2862ece44e7e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12454"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9a62365-4278-557f-ba76-caa31abe7869" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167129} {:db/id 17592186167130} {:db/id 17592186167131} {:db/id 17592186278417} {:db/id 17592186278418} {:db/id 17592186281387} {:db/id 17592186281388} {:db/id 17592186281492} {:db/id 17592186281494} {:db/id 17592186281496} {:db/id 17592186369894} {:db/id 17592186369908} {:db/id 17592186421235} {:db/id 17592186421237} {:db/id 17592186421241} {:db/id 17592186444618} {:db/id 17592186444619}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "99f84857-19d8-532f-b1f8-974d1ed142df" :step/math-academy-id 657087} {:db/id 17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3a45ce20-02a0-56e8-9b38-add2ba9480d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7733 :tutorial/title "The Fundamental Vector Product for a Horizontal Plane"} {:db/id 17592186362413 :tutorial/content "If we wish to find the flux through a tilted plane, we should first calculate the unit normal vector to this plane.

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: 1-x+y,\: 2y+8\rangle$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y-1$ such that $\textrm{Area}(S) = 2.$ 
Assume that we need to find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2(1-x+y)+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2+2x-2y+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186444620} :activity/id #uuid "0bdff687-f8d4-5855-9373-b5ab9e4534b8" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050188 :topic/id #uuid "34eb87b9-7036-55c0-88eb-1b1efbd11584" :topic/math-academy-id 3178} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186444620 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167127 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "51f5f2fd-94a6-51c3-ac48-99d59a93e907" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y+z" :db/id 17592186444605} {:answer/id #uuid "8524a039-125d-5c28-8aaa-2b417ce25d91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y+z" :db/id 17592186444606} {:answer/id #uuid "a0cc803d-28d2-5c8a-ad4d-e88ee6c149ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-y-z" :db/id 17592186444608} {:answer/id #uuid "ad810e29-dc47-543e-aeb1-8297ce882407" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z-x" :db/id 17592186444610} {:answer/id #uuid "e9761621-383d-53ec-8615-e110f65c1ad5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y+2z" :db/id 17592186444613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444610} :answer-field/id #uuid "63f86b8b-b32a-5de1-8bfa-b93d1b01899d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186163840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "44a48f57-f74b-5294-bb24-4cee5d89d1d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-161149" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(2z-(x+y)+(y-z)) \\  & =\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0ad1dc8f-1c73-5500-a47a-c0fda9ab766e"} {:db/id 17592186444622 :step/content {:db/id 17592186278421 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2720bb2d-ef3c-5bd3-b5d1-47e2a36e5b59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy+yz+xz" :db/id 17592186275834} {:answer/id #uuid "30f13b93-277e-5c15-b9c8-932581f5f992" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-2yz+xz" :db/id 17592186275912} {:answer/id #uuid "3b883b06-8332-53dc-bb7f-68fb90e59ae4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3xz-yz" :db/id 17592186275997} {:answer/id #uuid "74a4ce69-d793-5db1-9424-5b3b421ad0a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186276532} {:answer/id #uuid "8f857f74-c7bf-534b-90d2-dc5735bc9d12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-yz+2xz" :db/id 17592186276777}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186276777} :answer-field/id #uuid "74b1826a-ee9f-5272-9977-4058c1ea92ea" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277932}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fe4ccf73-c8f1-5e87-8e15-f27def60e911" :question/math-academy-id "q-161200" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}y\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [x]_{0}^{3} \\  & =-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "627a222e-9363-5b8b-b1ec-0730c89cfcbe" :question/math-academy-id "q-161193" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}y\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [x]_{0}^{3} \\  & =-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b60e2d93-3137-5009-9f82-8e66614f6b08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444624}} {:db/id 17592186444621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186444618 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23676b92-59ce-549e-bb44-0ce2c22aff60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186444601} {:answer/id #uuid "30a14e60-74d3-59a0-9d7c-8bfb0dc4a3c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444603} {:answer/id #uuid "8c7915a4-09c6-54d8-8b86-d3abcf6997b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444607} {:answer/id #uuid "ca06b212-b30b-58a7-bceb-f7e5db8c00f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444612} {:answer/id #uuid "f6e593f7-c2c1-5fc5-8a3d-c699694f0c1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444614} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ac4cbf3-d6da-5e60-8eb4-cf067330135d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444617}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2ae7b222-1017-5e06-9f85-8323117b3184" :question/math-academy-id "q-162158" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+2y+1$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{2}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0ad1dc8f-1c73-5500-a47a-c0fda9ab766e"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23676b92-59ce-549e-bb44-0ce2c22aff60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" For the surface $z=4$ for  $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.

Using the fact that $z=4$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨yz,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,4x,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =0\cdot 2 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5f59b70c-7621-5b4b-9951-a03dc596f197" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536930}} {:db/id 17592186536940 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281388 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ec4eec9-d885-5e59-95b5-8276383a1984" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186278724} {:answer/id #uuid "a1df3b0f-3419-5642-80d6-43333a0f05d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186280030} {:answer/id #uuid "cba2eb59-f72e-53a5-b7d3-0a0fb140ab74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280376} {:answer/id #uuid "d6581867-a9a5-5047-9e25-1ee87e16c985" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186280484} {:answer/id #uuid "e3fc824b-0743-5a05-ba40-9e5850d45c35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186280603}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280376} :answer-field/id #uuid "364a17d3-0c49-5f9e-932e-cfdc2819fcb3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280930}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "88097b92-017e-5e6e-bb41-84bae76dd7ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-162154" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x-y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{6}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

:question/math-academy-id "q-162154" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x-y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{6}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "76294a87-9654-50ec-a44d-a6393dfb7851"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ec4eec9-d885-5e59-95b5-8276383a1984" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}(4-2x)$ at the point $(1,\operatorname{ln}2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{ln}u,\,u=4-2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{4-2x}\cdot (-2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{4-2x} \\  & =-\frac{\cancel{2}}{\cancel{2}\cdot (2-x)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={-\frac{1}{2-x}|}_{x=1}=-\frac{1}{2-1}=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\operatorname{ln}2)$ is $m=-1.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\operatorname{ln}2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+\operatorname{ln}2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186233916 :question/id #uuid "3b0416da-07ab-52a1-b4f0-696bed0ae814" :question/math-academy-id "q-341676"} {:db/id 17592186253563 :question/id #uuid "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186278131}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\  & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xy(2x+y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{xy(2x+y)}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 2-(-y)\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7x}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278509 :question/id #uuid "d5fb8cb6-33d1-582b-8cf3-53ceebac82e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-161435"} {:db/id 17592186278522 :question/id #uuid "da0b12bf-561c-5907-8348-62e84bca5b63" :question/math-academy-id "q-161481" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15f8ea45-7189-5de7-b023-513085bc87a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi +\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}" :db/id 17592186275684} {:answer/id #uuid "1d8d5990-f27c-5d2a-8556-ade0d064ae64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi -\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{6}" :db/id 17592186275747} {:answer/id #uuid "9b81db63-fffe-50ae-abb4-769c30bdcdcc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi +\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{12}" :db/id 17592186276871} {:answer/id #uuid "bb7a2355-821a-5abf-ae21-cfb859e97e99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186277145} {:answer/id #uuid "e9752611-528c-5fdc-8927-863cf9474421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186277518}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275747} :answer-field/id #uuid "6db629ff-d6ea-571f-9225-53d34e230d79" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277919}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨1,\,0,\,y⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)$ for $-\pi \le x\le 0$ and $-x\le y\le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨1,\,0,\,y⟩{|}_{z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)} \\  & =⟨{{1}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨1,\,0,\,y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y))-0\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y))+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}{\int }_{-x}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=-x}^{y=0}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+0)-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡0+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}]}_{-\pi }^{0} \\  & =0-(-0+(-\pi )-\frac{(-\pi )^{3}}{6}) \\  & =\pi -\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278545 :question/id #uuid "d858f67e-e87d-5922-848f-1cf10db83bc5" :question/math-academy-id "q-161536" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198379 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aaa6b152-86d3-5f96-8a94-57f86a17a84d" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Flux Over a Surface"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b71688e-a084-50b0-8ee6-cfbf6ebd32af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3e-{e}^{-1}}{4}" :db/id 17592186275872} {:answer/id #uuid "4431028f-ab75-5b42-a52f-32fd75e489e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-1}-e}{2}" :db/id 17592186276079} {:answer/id #uuid "745d7976-0dbc-50a2-9490-bc45b40b9a87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5e+2{e}^{-1}}{4}" :db/id 17592186276530} {:answer/id #uuid "89b5e633-6fda-572c-a63c-6a89752bac4b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7e-{e}^{-1}}{2}" :db/id 17592186276721} {:answer/id #uuid "b0b62c25-f5f9-5ac7-a005-6cbd37efb361" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{3e+{e}^{-1}}{2}" :db/id 17592186277057}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "4431028f-ab75-5b42-a52f-32fd75e489e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-1}-e}{2}" :db/id 17592186276079} :answer-field/id #uuid "1b538e17-dfb5-54b8-b49d-76ddb3c1edcc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186277774}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z={e}^{x}$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x})={e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x})=0\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $F$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨y,\,x+z,\,0⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨y,\,x+z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={e}^{x}} \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x+{e}^{x}}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨y,\,x+z,\,0⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot ({e}^{x})-(x+{e}^{x})\cdot 0+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y{e}^{x})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-y{e}^{x})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[-\frac{{y}^{2}{e}^{x}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{[{e}^{x}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-1}-e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278546 :question/id #uuid "d38df384-c529-5d23-b152-2f8b3a09208a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161539"} {:db/id 17592186278547 :question/id #uuid $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 4$ and $-2\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{-2}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u+v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,-2\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u+v} \\  & =⟨u+v-v,\,2v-(u+v),\,uv⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\,v-u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,v-u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-1)+(v-u)\cdot (-1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-u-v+u+uv \\  & =uv-v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(uv-v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{-2}^{3}uv-v\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198610 :question/id #uuid "a3bcb9d3-050c-5ab9-bd2a-436465223147" :question/math-academy-id "q-161360" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f754a120-8886-56d3-b535-398f13b91c9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398529} {:answer/id #uuid "d28df103-ae23-5647-a506-1bc60c332868" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}+uv+{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398530} {:answer/id #uuid "e85142cb-e059-512c-8b7b-18eee7a8c253" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2uv" :db/id 17592186398531} {:answer/id #uuid "e433762d-59a0-5efb-bef2-7687d8583f2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398532} {:answer/id #uuid "3a53a3c7-e2f5-50e9-afd4-d3b986017cf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2(u+v)^{2}" :db/id 17592186398533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398531} :answer-field/id #uuid "185487e5-090f-5815-93b2-dfc0c983e691" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398528}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u+v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u+v} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2},\,(u+v)^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2},\,(u+v)^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot (-1)+{v}^{2}\cdot (-1)+(u+v)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =-{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}+2uv+{v}^{2} \\  & =2uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278495 :question/id #uuid "0bf481ef-95d3-5b3f-b324-29ecd57febda" :question/math-academy-id "q-161358" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10279bac-75c2-5820-bf33-84359cbf720e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7u+4v" :db/id 17592186275617} {:answer/id #uuid "397e53f3-63a0-518a-999e-8c3d8631bb27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4u+7v" :db/id 17592186275987} {:answer/id #uuid "897e0260-ef83-5fe5-9ee2-95ed9d4cd1a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7u+8v" :db/id 17592186276718} {:answer/id #uuid "bd3f2f9b-ef08-5972-b94d-02717ccd84df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8u-7v" :db/id 17592186277162} {:answer/id #uuid "ee6d4a87-66ae-58b1-806a-631ade59590d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7u-8v" :db/id 17592186277571}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275617} :answer-field/id #uuid "8692e3d1-c9bd-5cca-9274-6af9e13d6963" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277965}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=3x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 5$ and $-3\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=3u-2v} \\  & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\cdot ⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(3u-2v)\cdot (-3)+(-v)\cdot (2)+2u\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+6v-2v+2u \\  & =-7u+4v.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186278510 :question/id #uuid "279f5fbf-fc31-5667-8b25-7d1c25dc2d02" :question/math-academy-id "q-161441" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b5412c-a9ab-5d1e-8d26-9a4c8f27c8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2u+7v" :db/id 17592186275625} {:answer/id #uuid "16ffd34a-40d1-5df6-87ca-5595406b5509" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4u+v" :db/id 17592186275691} {:answer/id #uuid "85617ab2-8072-5a8d-9456-259cf0bef230" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4v-u" :db/id 17592186276672} {:answer/id #uuid "ce5a4f92-85cc-5237-ba98-a4e395360811" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2u+v" :db/id 17592186277305} {:answer/id #uuid "fe69b9d6-2d90-53f7-90a8-f4819b62096e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2u+4v" :db/id 17592186277710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275625} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a3b6104-863d-512e-9bea-c3b626c9b6e0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277943}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y-z,\,x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y-z,\,x+y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-2v} \\  & =⟨u,\,v-(u-2v),\,u+v⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\,3v-u,\,u+v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,3v-u,\,u+v⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-1)+(3v-u)\cdot 2+(u+v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-u+6v-2u+u+v \\  & =-2u+7v.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,y+2z,\,2x-y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=v-u} \\  & =⟨v-u,\,v+2(v-u),\,2u-v⟩ \\  & =⟨v-u,\,3v-2u,\,2u-v⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186398521 :question/id #uuid "d5e1155b-c484-5f31-a815-946d2d63d6df" :question/math-academy-id "q-161359" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c8c22e69-9068-5d72-8593-ce78861036f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398523} {:answer/id #uuid "2f4db3f6-9c97-526b-8cb2-065c8f5de466" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398524} {:answer/id #uuid "7b2e8a80-65c9-5d70-9b0e-0e801e7e718d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(u+v)^{2}" :db/id 17592186398525} {:answer/id #uuid "9f182d4d-0129-52ff-90b2-56e5acb487b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(u-v)^{2}" :db/id 17592186398526} {:answer/id #uuid "c1e4fd3a-37bb-5bcd-85c6-185c9a1d61c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}+uv-{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398527}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398523} :answer-field/id #uuid "396da9a4-de3b-5bd7-8b5e-dfc780e10bb9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398522}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)v\cdot (-1)+(u-v)u\cdot (1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-uv+{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}-uv+uv \\  & ={u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423120 :question/id #uuid "29805411-7a4c-51f7-893d-a0f3dc3cef10" :question/math-academy-id "q-161377"} {:db/id 17592186423123 :question/id #uuid "92e8ddd2-ccb6-5c20-b74b-2f784e857a55" :question/math-academy-id "q-161379" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b89c0b5-bd8b-5088-a053-0db9bc0fd31f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-uv" :db/id 17592186423085} {:answer/id #uuid "57bc1e11-c92f-5bf5-b1cd-bdfca274f1c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5uv" :db/id 17592186423091} {:answer/id #uuid "62a07ee3-0b12-5f4d-81e0-7183964e0136" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3u{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186423094} {:answer/id #uuid "876d48e1-3fb3-5bc6-88d3-a7e99ab5d29a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "uv+v" :db/id 17592186423100} {:answer/id #uuid "b65ee624-a7db-5060-ba14-007644627aeb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "uv-v" :db/id 17592186423104}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423091} :answer-field/id #uuid "dce1231b-682c-5119-8b60-1e600b81511c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423118}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=y-x$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $-3\le y\le 0.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,v-u⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,-3\le v\le 0\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=v-u} \\  & =⟨(u+v)^{2},\,(u-v)^{2},\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u+v)^{2},\,(u-v)^{2},\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u+v)^{2}\cdot 1+(u-v)^{2}\cdot (-1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =5uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}5uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423124 :question/id #uuid "ef91d27f-5ce3-5c48-b5b9-4ec732b3b2e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-161471" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "556660a7-ba40-5142-a23c-96cdb3bb38b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8u-23v" :db/id 17592186423090} {:answer/id #uuid "86aaa33f-073f-5b9c-b6ed-02e42f1370d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12u-v" :db/id 17592186423099} {:answer/id #uuid "8fa80cac-9ed0-54f2-a0fb-a71697486081" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8u+14v" :db/id 17592186423101} {:answer/id #uuid "9d9623af-3bba-5a0d-9c01-61a215703653" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5u-17v" :db/id 17592186423103} {:answer/id #uuid "b721d1da-8cb3-5423-bdff-f515271a77db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u-6v" :db/id 17592186423105}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423103} :answer-field/id #uuid "de6e4169-2fd0-5a0b-b7fe-172964aca58f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423119}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+z,\,2z,\,y+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-3y$ for $-1\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-3v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x+z,\,2z,\,y+z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-3v} \\  & =⟨u+u-3v,\,2(u-3v),\,v+u-3v⟩ \\  & =⟨2u-3v,\,2u-6v,\,u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨2u-3v,\,2u-6v,\,u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩ \\  & =(2u-3v)\cdot (-1)+(2u-6v)\cdot (3)+(u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u+3v+6u-18v+u-2v \\  & =5u-17v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5u-17v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{3}(5u-17v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $x=k(y,z),$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(y,z)=⟨k(y,z),\,y,\,z⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂k}{∂y},\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂k}{∂z},\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂k}{∂y} & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{∂k}{∂z} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|=⟨1,\,-\frac{∂k}{∂y},\,-\frac{∂k}{∂z}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

"4ec0f874-f1a4-5c03-8a41-bf094ee7ee97" :step/math-academy-id 44446 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199282}} {:db/id 17592186199300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199470 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive a general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Consider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle.
$$

Computing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the $\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize as follows:

- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$

- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - R\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf j$-component is positive.*

- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( P - Q\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "d20203b0-e15f-5061-ae68-16676ec933dc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7653 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Flux Over Cartesian Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "299c6f48-c761-519a-8d96-161fea9d6df0" :step/math-academy-id 44449 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199299}} {:db/id 17592186199306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199473 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=\left\langle (x-y)^2, \:(x+y)^2, \: 12xy \right\rangle
$$

 

through the surface $S$ defined by the Cartesian equation 

$$
z=2y-2x
$$

for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ 

For surfaces like this, substituting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain a parametrization 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: 2v-2u \right\rangle
$$

over the domain 

$$
D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 1, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

 

Recall that for a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$

{:db/id 17592186199300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199470 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive a general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Consider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle.
$$

Computing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the $\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize as follows:

- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$

- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - R\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf j$-component is positive.*

- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( P - Q\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "d20203b0-e15f-5061-ae68-16676ec933dc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7653 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Flux Over Cartesian Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "299c6f48-c761-519a-8d96-161fea9d6df0" :step/math-academy-id 44449 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199299}} {:db/id 17592186199299 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198392 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198034 :question/id #uuid "b81eb0cb-a740-5e86-921c-4baa8c179e55" :question/math-academy-id "e-12387"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "55cd2fdb-4cae-5f0b-bea0-e845d51190e1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049883}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198602} {:db/id 17592186198605} {:db/id 17592186278512} {:db/id 17592186278515} {:db/id 17592186278516} {:db/id 17592186278519} {:db/id 17592186373979} {:db/id 17592186401240} {:db/id 17592186401247} {:db/id 17592186401254} {:db/id 17592186423121} {:db/id 17592186423122}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral Using a Formula"} :step/id #uuid "4ec0f874-f1a4-5c03-8a41-bf094ee7ee97" :step/math-academy-id 44446 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199282}} {:db/id 17592186199470 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive a general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.

$$

$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)v\cdot (-1)+(u-v)u\cdot (1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-uv+{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}-uv+uv \\  & ={u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3c80623d-6de7-5b10-b86b-ce8711c212be" :step/next {:db/id 17592186431863}} {:db/id 17592186431863 :step/content {:db/id 17592186278510 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b5412c-a9ab-5d1e-8d26-9a4c8f27c8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2u+7v" :db/id 17592186275625} {:answer/id #uuid "16ffd34a-40d1-5df6-87ca-5595406b5509" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4u+v" :db/id 17592186275691} {:answer/id #uuid "85617ab2-8072-5a8d-9456-259cf0bef230" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4v-u" :db/id 17592186276672} {:answer/id #uuid "ce5a4f92-85cc-5237-ba98-a4e395360811" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2u+v" :db/id 17592186277305} {:answer/id #uuid "fe69b9d6-2d90-53f7-90a8-f4819b62096e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2u+4v" :db/id 17592186277710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275625} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a3b6104-863d-512e-9bea-c3b626c9b6e0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277943}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "279f5fbf-fc31-5667-8b25-7d1c25dc2d02" :question/math-academy-id "q-161441" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y-z,\,x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)v\cdot (-1)+(u-v)u\cdot (1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-uv+{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}-uv+uv \\  & ={u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}

over the domain

$$

$$

$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,3u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 5,\,-3\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=3u-2v} \\  & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\cdot ⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(3u-2v)\cdot (-3)+(-v)\cdot (2)+2u\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+6v-2v+2u \\  & =-7u+4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-7u+4v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(-7u+4v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "085a5662-c83a-5261-aadd-4e17a1724de2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186499585}} {:db/id 17592186499579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186401254 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8ffab214-a531-5f16-9548-4aba64a14e09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$∂z$ and $∂x$" :db/id 17592186401256} {:answer/id #uuid "27be7768-bf01-5a25-8f76-a7b3aa6827e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$∂x$ and $∂z$" :db/id 17592186401257} {:answer/id #uuid "ef0b36ca-8d50-5d13-b2d4-01dff2d1189e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$∂y$ and $∂z$" :db/id 17592186401258} {:answer/id #uuid "8c295efa-f53d-5757-9ea8-624ce01afe74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$∂x$ and $∂y$" :db/id 17592186401259} {:answer/id #uuid "401f8a2b-7596-5052-8ec8-449369280a45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$∂y$ and $∂x$" :db/id 17592186401260}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186401259} :answer-field/id #uuid "0585e533-2d5e-5fa5-b53e-85ce1c70e498" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186401255}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b2128236-dd4e-5cec-8d28-c07554df0f5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-161463" :question/problem "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u+v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u+v} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2},\,(u+v)^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2},\,(u+v)^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot (-1)+{v}^{2}\cdot (-1)+(u+v)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =-{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}+2uv+{v}^{2} \\  & =2uv.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}

$$
